tier_reason: summary.md compares four iohttpparser profiles with picohttpparser and vendored llhttp 9.3.1. The code is public (bench/bench_throughput_compare.c, scripts/run-throughput-median.sh), clang 22.1.0 is in toolchain.txt, and the flags come from the clang-release preset. The CPU model is not identified: host.txt lscpu shows only the generic QEMU/KVM vCPU string 'AMD EPYC Processor' (family 23 model 1, hypervisor KVM) with no host SKU or generation, so the numbers are first-party and fall short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: summary.md median req/s, 22 scenarios (21 common + 1 CONNECT). The best iohttpparser profile (stateful-strict alone gives the same count) beats llhttp in 16 and loses in 6. Wins include: req-headers 9.12M vs 7.87M (stateful-strict, 1.16x); resp-headers 12.08M vs 9.55M (stateful-lenient, 1.26x); hdr-value-ascii-clean 7.72M vs 5.16M (1.50x); hdr-count-32-minimal 2.89M vs 1.93M (1.50x); req-connect 14.32M vs 11.36M (1.26x). All ratios are derived from page data. llhttp wins req-small (22.91M vs best 18.36M, 0.80x), req-line-only, req-line-connect, hdr-name-heavy, hdr-uncommon-valid and hdr-count-04-minimal. picohttpparser is fastest in 21 of 22 scenarios. The exception is hdr-count-32-minimal, where stateful-strict edges it (2.89M vs 2.86M req/s).
corrections.workload: req/s, MiB/s and ns/req for 22 fixed scenarios: 21 common request, response and header-stress fixtures of 33-703 bytes, plus one 99-byte CONNECT request. Each timed iteration parses one complete single-message buffer from scratch. Every call re-initializes the parser: llhttp_init plus llhttp_finish, or a fresh ihtp state for the stateful profiles. Each run does 200,000 iterations after 1,000 warmups, and the reported figure is the median of 5 runs. The comparison covers four iohttpparser profiles against vendored picohttpparser and llhttp 9.3.1 (bench/bench_throughput_compare.c).
corrections.hardware: KVM guest with a generic QEMU 'AMD EPYC Processor' vCPU (family 23 model 1 stepping 2), 8 vCPU, 8 MiB L3; host CPU SKU not stated (per host.txt lscpu)
corrections.caveats: Zero-star, single-contributor project published in March 2026, with no independent adoption or third-party reproduction. The benchmark ran in a KVM guest whose lscpu shows only the generic 'AMD EPYC Processor' vCPU model, so the real host CPU is unknown and results carry shared-cloud noise. Each iteration parses one tiny (33-703 byte) standalone message with per-call parser init, which measures small-message latency rather than streaming throughput. Wins over llhttp are not uniform: llhttp wins 6 of 22 scenarios, including req-small (0.80x), three request-line cases and three header cases. picohttpparser is 1.07-2.46x faster than the best iohttpparser profile in 21 of 22 scenarios.

notes: All four numbers in the claim are on the page. The original claim was wrong that picohttpparser wins every scenario (iohttpparser edges it in hdr-count-32-minimal), and it understated llhttp's wins (req-small and three header scenarios also go to llhttp). The workload's '~8GiB per case keep-alive stream' is wrong: 200,000 iterations of a single 33-703 byte message is about 7-140 MB per case. License MIT, 0 stars, not fork or archived, last main commit 2026-03-14 (active); record metadata is correct.

tier_reason: The README bar chart (ada 188, servo url 664, CURL 1471 ns/URL, top100 dataset) is first-party and gives only 'Apple MacBook 2022 with LLVM 14', with no chip or flags. The peer-reviewed paper (Nizipli & Lemire, SPE 54(5) 2024, arXiv 2311.10533) shows Ada beating curl 7.81.0 and names the CPUs (AMD EPYC 7262, Apple M2) and compilers (GCC 11, Apple/LLVM 14). The paper's code is public (benchmarks/bench.cpp, benchdata target), but no optimization flags are stated, so the evidence is B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, top100 dataset: ada 188 ns/URL vs servo url 664 ns/URL vs CURL 1471 ns/URL. That is about 7.8x faster than curl and 3.5x faster than servo rust-url (derived from page data). The README also quotes State of Node.js Performance 2023: after Node.js adopted Ada, 'Some results could reach up to an improvement of 400%'. The peer-reviewed paper reports Ada above 3M URLs/s (AMD EPYC 7262) and 5M URLs/s (Apple M2), against about 0.5M and nearly 1M URLs/s for curl. On top100 it needs 8x fewer instructions than curl.
corrections.hardware: README: 'Apple MacBook 2022' with LLVM 14, chip not stated. The linked paper's Apple system is an Apple M2 3.0 GHz MacBook Air (2022) with Apple/LLVM 14, and it also tests an AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen 2, 3.4 GHz) with GCC 11.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README: LLVM 14, optimization flags not stated. Paper: GCC 11 (EPYC 7262) and Apple/LLVM 14 (M2), flags not stated. Ada's cmake/ada-flags.cmake defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release when no build type is given.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.85k stars; README names Node.js, Redpanda, Kong, Telegram, DataDog and Cloudflare Workers as users
corrections.caveats: The README benchmark is first-party. Hardware is given only as 'Apple MacBook 2022' with LLVM 14, and no flags are listed. It is backed by a peer-reviewed paper (Nizipli & Lemire, 'Parsing Millions of URLs per Second', Software: Practice and Experience 54(5), 2024, https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.3296) whose C++ results appear only as bar charts. The comparison is not like-for-like: curl follows RFC 3986, not WHATWG, and the paper warns 'direct comparisons must be done with care'. On top100, curl rejects 130 URLs versus 26 for Ada. The 400% Node.js figure is a Node 16-to-20 URL benchmark from a third-party blog post, not an isolated parser comparison.

notes: README numbers and the 400% Node.js quote are verified. The State of Node.js Performance 2023 post contains the 400% sentence. The ada_analysis raw Google Benchmark JSON for an Apple machine (overall/m2/top100.json: 3.4 GHz, curl 7.87.0) shows 239 ns/URL for ada (162 for url_aggregator) vs 1234 ns/URL for curl, which fits the README claim but is not the same run. ClickHouse, Adguard and Internet Archive were removed from usage: the README and ada-url.com do not list them, and ClickHouse's contrib/ has no ada. License is dual Apache-2.0/MIT (LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT; README: 'Apache License 2.0 as well as the MIT license'). Last commit 2026-09-20; the repo is not a fork and not archived.

tier_reason: The README section compares fasthttp against net/http with first-party go test output. The benchmark code is public (server_timing_test.go, client_timing_test.go). The CPU is only the generic 'Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.20GHz' string and no Go version is stated, so this is first-party evidence with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'fasthttp server is up to 6 times faster than net/http' and 'fasthttp client is up to 4 times faster'. The 'up to 10x' is the GitHub repo description, not the README. Server, GOMAXPROCS=4, 10K reqs/conn: net/http 2179 ns/op (2386 B/op, 21 allocs/op) vs fasthttp 451.4 ns/op (0 B/op, 0 allocs/op), about 4.8x. The same case at GOMAXPROCS=1 is 7151 vs 1422 ns/op, about 5.0x. The best server row is 14010 vs 2208 ns/op, about 6.3x (GOMAXPROCS=1, 2 reqs/conn, 10K clients). Client end-to-end is about 2.0-2.3x over TCP and 4.9-11.7x in-memory, peaking at 31010 vs 2645 ns/op with 1000 in-memory conns at GOMAXPROCS=4. All ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.workload: Go testing benchmarks (server_timing_test.go, client_timing_test.go; go test -bench -benchmem -benchtime=10s) at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 4. Server tests send a GET that gets a small fake response over an in-memory fake listener and connections, with no real network. They cover 1/2/10/10K requests per connection, and 1/2/10/100 requests per connection with 10K clients, comparing fasthttp.Server with net/http's http.Server. Client tests run an end-to-end GET over TCP (1/10/100 conns) and in-memory (1-1000 conns; fasthttp also 10K).
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is first-party (the project's own go test code) with partial methodology. The CPU is only the generic 'Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.20GHz' string, and no Go version is given. The server benchmarks use in-memory fake connections, so they measure the whole server path (parsing, allocation, handler dispatch) without real network I/O. They do not isolate HTTP parsing. The 'up to 10x' headline is the repo description; the README text says up to 6x (server) and 4x (client), although its in-memory client rows reach about 11.7x. The README itself warns that for most cases net/http is the better choice.

notes: All quoted server numbers match the README. The only misstatement was attributing 'up to 10x' to the README; it comes from the repo description, and the README client in-memory rows support up to about 11.7x (derived). TechEmpower R23 raw data (results/round23/ph.json, totalRequests/15 s, derived) is mixed. fasthttp-prefork reaches about 14.6M plaintext rps vs 2.0M for go-pgx-prefork and 1.6M for go (net/http). Non-prefork fasthttp manages only about 0.57M plaintext rps, but beats go in JSON (0.58M vs 0.39M). So no tier upgrade from TechEmpower. Metadata is correct: MIT, 23,476 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not fork, not archived.
